title: Bai Juyi's 'Old Charcoal-Seller' (Mai tan weng), New Yuefu no. 32
short: A satire from Bai Juyi's 'New Yuefu' series (c. 809) against the 'palace market', by which eunuchs seized goods for the court.
body: 賣炭翁 Mai tan weng, 'The Old Charcoal-Seller', is no. 32 of the fifty 新樂府 Xin yuefu ('New Music Bureau Ballads') that Bai Juyi (772-846) wrote around 809, when he was a censor at court. Each poem has a subtitle stating its target; this one is 苦宮市也, 'suffering under the palace market'. In his preface Bai said the series was written for the ruler, ministers, people, things and events, 'not for literature', and he wanted the meaning plain. Waley printed it in A Hundred and Seventy Chinese Poems (1918) with the subtitle 'A Satire against Kommandatur', a pointed allusion to wartime German military requisitioning that the archive's text omits. Waley's introduction calls these poems 'moral tales in verse'.

title: the Southern Mountain (Nanshan): the Zhongnan range
short: The Zhongnan range south of Chang'an, which supplied the capital with timber and charcoal.
body: 伐薪燒炭南山中, 'cutting wood and burning charcoal in the Southern Mountains'. 南山 Nanshan is the Zhongnan range, some tens of kilometres south of the Tang capital Chang'an (modern Xi'an), a region of forests, Daoist and Buddhist retreats and estates such as Wang Wei's Wangchuan. Charcoal was the main fuel for heating in the capital's winters, and woodcutters from the hills carried it in by cart. The poem's realism lies in such specific detail of labour and place.

title: the charcoal-burner's face
short: The old man's face, hair and hands are marked by his trade, an unadorned portrait in the plain style Bai Juyi favoured.
body: 滿面塵灰煙火色，兩鬢蒼蒼十指黑: 'face full of dust and ash, the colour of smoke and fire; temples grizzled grey, ten fingers black'. Bai Juyi was famous for writing so plainly that, according to a later anecdote, he read his poems to an old woman and revised anything she could not understand. The two parallel lines move from face to hair to hands. Waley keeps the parallelism closely, including 'his ten fingers are black', a literal rendering of 十指黑.

title: the poor man's paradox
greek: 可憐身上衣正單，心憂炭賤願天寒
short: Thinly clad, the old man still wishes for colder weather, because cold raises the price of charcoal: the poem's bitterest irony.
body: 可憐身上衣正單，心憂炭賤願天寒, 'pitiable: the clothes on his body are just a single layer, yet, worrying that charcoal will be cheap, he wishes the weather cold'. 可憐 kelian, 'pitiable, alas', is the poet's comment, which Waley translates 'alas'. The couplet is often singled out by Chinese critics as the heart of the poem: poverty forces the man to wish for his own suffering. Waley's 'a coat without lining' is a precise rendering of 單 dan, 'single-layered'. Note that Waley here writes 'coal' for charcoal, as also in the last line.

title: the snowfall and frozen ruts
short: His wish is granted: a foot of snow falls, and he drives his cart at dawn over frozen ruts into the city.
body: 夜來城外一尺雪，曉駕炭車輾冰轍, 'overnight a foot of snow outside the city; at dawn he drives the charcoal cart over frozen ruts'. A Chinese foot (chi) was about 30 cm in the Tang. The snow seems to answer his hope, setting up the reversal that follows. Waley's punctuation with dashes (here and in 'Oxen,--weary; man,--hungry') imitates the clipped, list-like syntax of the Chinese seven-character lines.

anchor: to the south of the Market
title: the market gate of Chang'an
short: Chang'an had two walled markets, East and West; he rests in the mud outside a market's south gate.
body: 市南門外泥中歇, 'outside the market's south gate he rests in the mud'. Tang Chang'an was laid out on a grid with two official markets, the East Market and the West Market, each walled with gates that opened and closed at set hours. The detail of mud (snow melted by the high sun) brings out the man's exhaustion, while the market itself is the place where he hopes for a fair sale. Waley's capitalised 'Gate' and 'Market' mark them as named places.

title: the 'yellow-robed envoy' and the boy in white
short: The yellow-robed envoy was a palace eunuch; the 'white shirt' boy was his attendant, both agents of the palace market.
body: 翩翩兩騎來是誰？黃衣使者白衫兒: 'Prancing, two riders: who comes? An envoy in yellow robes, a lad in a white shirt'. The 'yellow-robed envoys' (黃衣使者) were the palace eunuchs who bought goods for the court; the 'white shirts' were their hangers-on, recruited from the city's idle youth. Waley's 'A public official' is accurate in function but loses the specific reference to eunuchs, whose growing power was a major political issue in Bai Juyi's day. The rhetorical question ('Who can it be coming?') mimics the ballad style of folk songs.

title: warrant and edict (chi 敕)
short: They show a document and claim an imperial edict, so the seizure cannot be resisted.
body: 手把文書口稱敕, 'in hand they hold documents, in their mouths they call it an edict'. 敕 chi is an imperial order. The line implies a gap between the paper they wave and the authority they claim: the eunuchs invoke the emperor's name for what is in effect robbery. Waley's 'on their tongues--the words of an order' keeps the contrast of hand and mouth.

title: 'to the north': towards the palace
short: The palace city lay at the north end of Chang'an, so 'north' means the cart is taken to the court.
body: 迴車叱牛牽向北, 'they turn the cart, curse the ox, and lead it north'. Chang'an's palace city and imperial city occupied the north centre of the grid, with the markets to the south-west and south-east, so 'north' needs no further explanation for a Tang reader: the charcoal goes to the palace. Waley's plural 'oxen' differs from the singular ox usually understood (the Chinese does not mark number).

title: 'a thousand jin': weight, not pieces
short: The Chinese gives the cart's weight, over a thousand catties (jin); Waley's 'pieces' is a loose or mistaken rendering.
body: 一車炭，重千餘斤, 'one cart of charcoal, weighing over a thousand jin'. 斤 jin, the catty, was a unit of weight (about 600 g in the Tang, so the load was over half a tonne). Waley's 'More than a thousand pieces' treats jin as a counter for pieces. The sense, the size of the load and the value of the whole winter's labour, comes through, but readers should note the change. The short exclamatory lines (three characters each in some texts) break the seven-character rhythm for emphasis.

title: the palace market (gongshi 宮市)
short: Under the 'palace market', eunuch buyers took goods for the court at nominal prices; it was much resented and was suspended in the reforms of 805.
body: 宮使驅將惜不得, 'the palace envoys drive it away, and he cannot grudge it'. The 宮市 gongshi system, in which eunuch commissioners bought supplies for the palace in the capital's markets, degenerated in the late eighth century into open extortion. Han Yu's Veritable Records of Emperor Shunzong records the abuses, including a story of a peasant whose firewood was taken in a similar way, and the system was suspended in the reforms of 805, though some editions read the subtitle 官市 'official market' and the abuses the poem describes evidently remained a live issue. Bai Juyi's poem, written a few years later, attacks the practice as an example of the court's indifference to ordinary people. Waley's 'If officials choose' generalises the line into a statement about power.

anchor: Half a piece of red silk
title: payment in silk
short: The payment, half a bolt of red silk gauze and ten feet of damask tied to the ox's head, is far below the value of the load.
body: 半匹紅綃（紗）一丈綾，繫向牛頭充炭直, 'half a bolt of red gauze and a zhang of damask, tied to the ox's head as the price of the charcoal'. Silk cloth was a form of currency in Tang China, and taxes and salaries were often paid in it, so payment in silk was not itself unusual; but half a bolt and a zhang (about three metres, Waley's 'a single yard') were worth much less than a cartload of charcoal, and useless to a man who needed food and warm clothes. 'Tied to the ox's head' (Waley: 'the oxen's collar') shows contempt: the payment is attached to the animal, not given to the man. The poem ends without comment, letting the fact speak, as Bai's satirical programme required.
